brunswick.one_liner: A Potomac riverside railroad town the B&O built, still a working commuter-rail stop into Washington, DC.

fun_facts.text: Before it was Brunswick it was Berlin, platted in 1787 by Leonard Smith. The name changed at the 1890 incorporation because Maryland's Eastern Shore already had a Berlin and the mail kept getting confused.
The B&O's Brunswick classification yards, completed in 1907, ran five miles long and were the largest and most modern in the nation serving a single railroad at the time.
The B&O rail yard boosted the population past 5,000 and made Brunswick virtually a company town.
The area was once nicknamed Eel Town, because Native people fished for eel in the Potomac here.
Country legend Patsy Cline performed at the Moose Lodge in Brunswick, where she met her first husband, Gerald Cline.

insights.text: The real reason to come is the C&O Canal: Brunswick is a quiet riverside trailhead onto the flat towpath, with parking on hand, less hectic than crowded Harpers Ferry just upriver.
Inside the Heritage Museum, climb to the third floor for the HO-scale model of the B&O's Metropolitan line from DC to Brunswick in the late 1950s, including the old classification yards.
You can arrive carless on the MARC train, but it runs weekdays only, so save a Brunswick trip for a Monday-through-Friday if the train is your ride.

burkittsville.one_liner: A tiny 19th-century agricultural village under South Mountain, looking much as it did in 1862, and known as Blair Witch country.

faq.a: Two things: it is the named setting of the 1999 horror film The Blair Witch Project, and it is a near-intact Civil War-era streetscape beside the 1862 Battle of Crampton's Gap. The town calls itself a time capsule of the 19th century.

faq.q: Was The Blair Witch Project actually filmed here?
faq.a: The film is set near Burkittsville and the opening trip scenes were shot in town, but the fictional Black Hills Forest is Seneca Creek State Park, about 25 miles west.

faq.q: Is it walkable, and what should I see?
faq.a: Yes. At about half a square mile it is a few-minute grid centered on Main Street and two 1800s churches. Pick up the Civil War walking-tour brochure at the town bulletin board, The Bugle, on East Main Street across from the post office.

faq.q: What is there to do nearby?
faq.a: Gathland State Park sits about a mile up the mountain, with the War Correspondents Memorial Arch and Appalachian Trail access. The South Mountain Heritage Society museum opens the first Saturday of the month, April through September, 10 to 3.

fun_facts.text: The village began as Harley's Post Office in 1824 and was renamed for Henry Burkitt after founder Joshua Harley died in 1828. It incorporated in 1894.
The 2020 census counted just 142 residents, down from 151 in 2010, on about 0.46 square miles.
During the September 14, 1862 Battle of Crampton's Gap, both town churches and the adjacent schoolhouse became hospitals for more than 300 wounded from both armies.

Just above town, the War Correspondents Memorial Arch was built in 1896 by Civil War correspondent George Alfred 'Gath' Townsend, and is often called the only monument in the world dedicated to journalists killed in combat.
Nearly all of Burkittsville is a National Register historic district, listed November 20, 1975, with about 70 contributing structures across 300 acres.

insights.text: The real reason to come is the streetscape: the David Arnold House (original portion 1798), the Resurrection German Reformed Church (1829-30, which served as a Sixth Corps hospital), and St. Paul's Lutheran (1859) stand much as they did in 1862.

Drive the mile up to Gathland State Park and pair the arch with Appalachian Trail access at Crampton's Gap. The heritage-society museum is open first Saturdays April through September, so time your visit if you want inside.
There is a roadside gravity hill on Gapland Road where a car in neutral seems to roll uphill. It is an optical illusion, but a fun stop on the way to the park.
Come for the history and the mountain, not the film: this is a lived-in village, and the movie's woods are actually Seneca Creek State Park, about 25 miles west.

emmitsburg.one_liner: A small Catoctin-foothills town that is both a major Catholic pilgrimage destination and a quiet college town.

faq.a: Two major Catholic pilgrimage sites: the National Shrine Grotto of Our Lady of Lourdes and the Basilica and National Shrine of Saint Elizabeth Ann Seton, the first native-born U.S. citizen canonized a saint. It is also home to Mount St. Mary's University and the national firefighters memorial.

faq.q: What should I see if I only have a couple of hours?
faq.a: Walk the Grotto of Lourdes grounds at Mount St. Mary's, then visit the Seton Shrine basilica in town. They are a short drive apart.

faq.q: Can I visit the National Fallen Firefighters Memorial?
faq.a: Yes. Memorial Park on the National Emergency Training Center campus is open to the public sunrise to sunset daily. Effective May 7, 2025, visitors over 16 need REAL ID-compliant identification to enter the campus.
Small. The 2020 census recorded 2,770 residents, just south of the Mason-Dixon line and about 12 miles from Gettysburg.

fun_facts.text: The Grotto of Lourdes here is the oldest U.S. replica of the Lourdes shrine, built about 17 years after the 1858 apparitions to St. Bernadette in France.

Saint Elizabeth Ann Seton founded the first U.S. congregation of religious sisters in Emmitsburg in 1809, whose school was the country's first free Catholic school. In 1975 she became the first person born in what is now the United States to be canonized; her remains are interred at the Emmitsburg basilica.
Mount St. Mary's, founded in 1808, houses the second-oldest Catholic seminary in the United States, after St. Mary's in Baltimore.
The Grotto's 95-foot tower is topped by a 25-foot gold-leafed bronze statue of Mary, a landmark for miles.
The National Fallen Firefighters Memorial was constructed here in 1981 and designated a National Memorial by Congress in 1990; the national memorial weekend is held each May.

insights.text: The real reason to come is the Grotto: it draws more than 400,000 visitors a year, and it stays peaceful on weekday mornings.
The Seton Shrine ranks among the top eight Catholic pilgrimage destinations in the country, and the basilica and grounds are open to visitors, not just pilgrims.
Pair the visit with Gettysburg, about 12 miles north across the state line, or Catoctin Mountain Park nearby, and treat Emmitsburg as the calm base between them.

frederick.one_liner: A walkable historic downtown of clustered church spires, antique-row shops, and a creekside linear park reclaimed from a flood channel.

faq.q: What is Downtown Frederick known for?
faq.a: A 40-square-block historic district, one of the largest contiguous historic districts on the East Coast, home to more than 200 specialty shops, galleries, breweries, distilleries, and restaurants. Its skyline of church steeples earned the city the nickname City of Clustered Spires.

Yes. The American Planning Association named it a Great Neighborhood in 2010, a dense mixed-use grid where housing, restaurants, museums, shops, and government offices all sit within walking distance.
Downtown has multiple garages plus metered and street parking. The Frederick Visitor Center, with free parking, sits at 151 S. East Street.

faq.q: What should I make time for?
faq.a: Carroll Creek Linear Park, threading the historic district with public art, fountains, and creekside dining. The National Museum of Civil War Medicine and the Delaplaine Arts Center are both downtown stops.

fun_facts.text: The nickname City of Clustered Spires comes from John Greenleaf Whittier's poem about Barbara Fritchie: "The clustered spires of Frederick stand / Green-walled by the hills of Maryland."
In July 1864, Confederate forces under Jubal Early occupied Frederick and extorted a $200,000 ransom from its citizens in exchange for not razing the city.

The Community Bridge over Carroll Creek looks like an ivy-covered old stone bridge, but it is a trompe-l'oeil mural painted flat onto a plain concrete bridge by artist William Cochran between 1993 and 1998, with over 3,000 simulated stones.
Carroll Creek Park began as a flood-control project; the city's initial roughly $11 million investment leveraged about $150 million in new construction, infill development, and historic renovation.
Francis Scott Key and Roger B. Taney both practiced law in Frederick; Barbara Fritchie is buried in the city's Mount Olivet Cemetery.

insights.text: The real draw is Carroll Creek: walk the path along the water, not just the storefronts, and look closely at the Community Bridge, where the stonework is painted, not built.
Come after dark in winter for Sailing Through the Winter Solstice, when lighted sailboats line the creek; warmer months bring live music, fountains, and the Color on the Creek water gardens.
Park once and stay on foot. The district is a compact 40-square-block grid, so a garage near Market or Patrick Street puts shops, restaurants, breweries, and the creek all within an easy walk.

middletown.one_liner: A historic National Road valley town set between two mountain ranges, anchored by a walkable Main Street.

faq.a: Its historic Main Street and Civil War heritage: both armies passed through on the way to the battles of South Mountain and Antietam, and the town opened its churches and homes to care for the wounded. It sits in the Middletown Valley between the Catoctin Mountains and South Mountain.

Yes. The historic district holds Federal and Greek Revival architecture, and Main Street Middletown offers self-guided Heritage Walking Tours alongside Civil War Trails and local history wayside exhibits.

faq.q: What is there to do nearby?
faq.a: Walk the historic Main Street, then head west to Civil War sites like South Mountain State Battlefield Park and Gathland State Park. South Mountain Creamery is a nearby ice cream stop, and Orchid Cellar meadery sits just north of town.
No. Middletown had a population of 4,943 at the 2020 census, a small valley town rather than a city.

fun_facts.text: Michael Jesserong sold the first town lots in 1767, the date officially marked as Middletown's founding; Main Street later spread west with construction of the National Pike through town in 1806.
The town reportedly got its name from sitting midway between two ranges, the Catoctin Mountains to the east and South Mountain to the west, in the Middletown Valley.

In July 1864 Confederate Gen. Jubal Early demanded a $5,000 ransom or the town would be burned; townspeople paid $1,500 and scrambled for the rest, but the town was spared when Early turned his attention to ransoming Frederick and marching on Washington.

Charles F. Main opened an ice cream shop and factory at 14 West Main Street in 1922; Main's Quality Ice Cream drew generations of Marylanders until it closed in 1969, and the building has been The Main Cup restaurant since 2007.
Charlie 'King Kong' Keller, a five-time MLB All-Star who played in four World Series as a New York Yankees outfielder, was born on a farm near Middletown in 1916.

insights.text: Come for the Main Street walk, then keep driving west: the road climbs toward South Mountain State Battlefield and Gathland State Park, which is the real draw beyond town.
Eat at The Main Cup; it occupies the old Main's Ice Cream factory and shop, so the building itself is part of the town's story rather than just a meal stop.

The valley views are the point. A young George Washington reportedly called the Middletown Valley one of the most beautiful places he had ever seen, and Andrew Jackson one of the most favored spots on earth; it still reads as open farm country framed by mountains.

mount-airy.one_liner: A two-county railroad town on Parr's Ridge, now a calm commuter community with a walkable historic Main Street.

faq.q: What is Mount Airy known for?
faq.a: Its B&O Railroad roots on Parr's Ridge and a compact historic Main Street of locally owned shops and eateries. The town uniquely straddles two counties, Carroll and Frederick.
Yes. The historic Main Street is easily wandered on foot, lined with shops, cafes, and restaurants for an afternoon stroll.

faq.q: How far is it from Baltimore and DC?
faq.a: About 40 minutes by car from Baltimore and roughly an hour from Washington, DC.

faq.q: Anything for beer and wine lovers?
faq.a: Two local breweries anchor downtown: Frey's, a farm brewery in a 200-year-old barn, and Liquidity Aleworks in the old bank building on Main Street. Black Ankle Vineyards is just outside town.

fun_facts.text: Mount Airy sits in two counties at once. When Carroll County set its permanent boundaries in 1837, the town was divided between Carroll and Frederick.
About a mile south of town, four counties meet at one point: Carroll, Frederick, Howard, and Montgomery, at the source of the South Branch of the Patapsco River.

Because the town sits at about 830 feet on Parr's Ridge, the early B&O Railroad built four inclined planes that lifted locomotives and cars uphill with horses and steam winches, before abandoning them in 1839 for an alternate route known as the Mount Airy Loop.
The town owes its name to an Irish B&O brakeman whose ears were freezing in the keen, cold air crossing Parr's Ridge; he suggested 'Mount Airy' would be appropriate, and it stuck.
Notable residents include NBA player Josh Boone, NFL lineman Rob Havenstein, and Racing Hall of Fame thoroughbred trainer John M. Gaver Sr.

insights.text: Come for the Main Street itself: park once and wander the locally owned shops, cafes, and taverns rather than treating the town as a quick stop off the highway.
The brewery scene leans on character buildings worth seeing in person: Frey's occupies a 200-year-old barn and Liquidity Aleworks sits in the town's old bank building.
Make it a day trip by pairing downtown with the surrounding vineyards: Black Ankle, Linganore, and Elk Run all carry Mount Airy addresses in the rolling hills around town.

myersville.one_liner: A small rural town at the foot of South Mountain, the everyday gateway to its ridge trails.

faq.a: It is a small rural town at the base of South Mountain, best known as a quiet gateway to the Appalachian Trail, Greenbrier State Park, and the ridge above. The Myersville area is also the source of Catoctin Creek.
The town covers only about one square mile and is almost entirely residential, with a small old core along Main Street. The real draws are on the mountain west of town, not downtown.
Most come for the hiking. The Appalachian Trail along South Mountain and Greenbrier State Park's lake and trails are reached from US 40 just west of town.

faq.q: Where do I park for the trails?
faq.a: There is a lot at Greenbrier State Park off Route 40, where the Appalachian Trail enters the park on Bartman's Hill Trail. A separate AT parking lot sits on Route 40 about a quarter mile east of Greenbrier.
Myersville sits on Interstate 70 between Frederick and Hagerstown, with US 40 just to the northeast; I-70 was extended through town in 1968.

fun_facts.text: Myersville was incorporated by an Act of the Maryland Legislature in March 1904, when it had a population of 150.
An electric trolley reached town as the Myersville and Catoctin Railway around 1898, operated as part of the Hagerstown and Frederick system that linked the two cities.
On January 4, 1919, a large fire destroyed many shops and buildings in the center of town.

In the early morning of October 24, 2002, D.C. snipers John Allen Muhammad and Lee Boyd Malvo were taken into custody while asleep in their car at an Interstate 70 rest stop near Myersville, after a truck driver called 911 to report the vehicle.
Two area properties, the Peter of P. Grossnickel Farm and the Henry Brandenburg House, are listed on the National Register of Historic Places.

insights.text: The real reason to stop is the ridge above town: from the Appalachian Trail at Annapolis Rock and Black Rock, reached from Route 40, you get sweeping westward views over Greenbrier Lake and the valley.

If you want the trails without a long approach, start at Greenbrier State Park off Route 40, with its 42-acre lake and almost eleven miles of paths that connect up to the AT, rather than parking in town.
Treat Myersville as a base or a quick bite off I-70, not a downtown destination; it is overwhelmingly rural and residential, with the draws on the mountain west of town.

new-market.one_liner: A compact National Pike town laid out in the 1790s, long known as Maryland's antiques capital along a walkable Main Street.

rosemont.one_liner: A tiny incorporated village above Brunswick, founded in 1953 to keep itself residential and quiet.

fun_facts.text: Rosemont incorporated itself in 1953 to block a mill: when the Southern States Cooperative planned to build one, 55 residents petitioned for a Circuit Court injunction, and on the last day of that month the Governor signed a bill incorporating the village.

At the village's first election on May 2, 1953, the first order of business for the new burgess and commissioners was establishing a zoning commission and ordinance, locking in its residential character.
Rosemont is home to a Meyer Kaplon steel house, one of the avant-garde models displayed in the U.S. Steel exhibit at the 1933 Chicago World's Fair.
The village contains two early-20th-century Sears, Roebuck mail-order houses: the Dr. J. G. F. Smith house on Petersville Road and the James Rau house on Rosemont Drive.
Covering just 0.56 square miles at about 495 feet elevation, Rosemont is served by four state highways (MD 17, 79, 464, and 871) despite its small size.

insights.text: The real reason to come is the outlook: the village faces rolling farmland and the mountains contoured by Harpers Ferry Gap, so it rewards a drive-through at golden hour rather than expecting things to do.

Park and base yourself in Brunswick, not Rosemont. From there the C&O Canal towpath is right at hand and the Appalachian Trail diverges at Weverton about three miles west; Rosemont itself has no parking lots or trailheads.
If you skip the car, the MARC Brunswick Line runs from Washington's Union Station to Brunswick on weekdays, putting you a short uphill walk from Rosemont without driving.

thurmont.one_liner: A small mountain-gateway town below Catoctin's ridges, equal parts historic Main Street and trailhead.

fun_facts.text: The town was incorporated as Mechanicstown in 1751; in 1894 the name was changed to Thurmont, from the German 'thur' (gateway) and the Latin 'mons' (mountain), roughly 'Gateway to the Mountains.'
Residents' first choice for the new name was 'Blue Mountain City,' but the Post Office rejected it as too similar to an existing town, so Thurmont eventually prevailed.
Nearby Catoctin Furnace was built in 1774 and was operating as a blast furnace by 1776, casting cannonballs as ammunition for the American Revolution.
Thomas Johnson, who built Catoctin Furnace with his brothers, became Maryland's first state governor in 1777 and later an Associate Justice of the U.S. Supreme Court.
Catoctin Colorfest began in 1963 as a nature walk and grew into a juried festival that draws about 125,000 people each October.

insights.text: The real reason to come is the park, not the town: Catoctin Mountain Park is free and laces together short overlook hikes like Thurmont Vista and Chimney Rock.
Take the short trail to the Blue Blazes Whiskey Still for a quick, genuine piece of Prohibition-era park history.
Pair the two parks: hike Catoctin's ridges, then cross to Cunningham Falls for the cascade and a swim at the Hunting Creek Lake beach.
Visit on Colorfest weekend only if you want the crowd; admission is free but parking is paid, so use the free shuttle rather than circling Main Street.

urbana.one_liner: A fast-grown planned suburb on a colonial-era crossroads, where a Civil War cavalry ball is still the famous story.

fun_facts.text: On September 8, 1862, Confederate cavalry general J.E.B. Stuart held a ball at the Landon House; word came that Union cavalry was near, the men rode off to repel it, then returned and the dancing resumed.
The Landon House was built in 1754 near the Rappahannock River in Virginia and moved north by barge in 1846, later serving as a girls' schoolhouse and, by 1854, the Landon Military Academy.
Urbana's population grew about 45% in a single decade, from 9,175 in 2010 to 13,304 in 2020, after the modern community began developing around 1999.
The area was first settled in 1730, two and a half centuries before the master-planned community that now defines it.
After the 1862 ball, the Landon House became a field hospital, and soldiers' wall sketches survive; Union troops reportedly drew Lincoln twice the size of the Confederates' Davis and Stuart.

insights.text: The real draw is the layered contrast: a community built around 1999 sitting on ground settled in 1730, with the 1754 Landon House nearby where the September 1862 cavalry ball happened.
Pair Urbana with Sugarloaf Mountain and the C&O Canal nearby; the same Attack-on-Washington Civil War trail ties them together, so it reads as one outing rather than a single stop.
Don't expect a historic main-street downtown; the center is a newer planned community, and the genuinely old fabric is the Zion Church and cemetery and the relocated Landon House.

walkersville.one_liner: A quiet residential town about 5 miles northeast of Frederick, best known for its volunteer-run heritage railroad.

faq.a: The Walkersville Southern Railroad, a volunteer-run heritage line that offers scenic excursion trips through the countryside northeast of Frederick.

faq.q: Where is it and how big is it?
faq.a: About 5 miles northeast of the City of Frederick. The town covers roughly 4.36 square miles and had 6,156 residents at the 2020 census.

faq.q: Can you ride the scenic train, and when?
faq.a: Yes. Excursion trains run Saturdays and Sundays in May, June, September and October, and Saturdays only in July and August, with special-event trains at other times. The ride runs a little over an hour.
Yes. The railroad runs family outings including Santa trains during the Christmas season, and there is a small railroad museum by the depot.

fun_facts.text: Walkersville incorporated in 1892. It was tiny for a long time: just 160 people lived here in 1880.

The Walkersville Southern Railroad runs on a 6.72-mile line whose track and structures were originally built by the Frederick and Pennsylvania Line Railroad, which opened October 8, 1872, and was leased to the Pennsylvania Railroad from January 1, 1875.

The excursion line crosses the Monocacy River on a bridge rebuilt after Hurricane Agnes washed out the original in 1972; tourist trains began running to the river in 1995, and the new bridge was completed in March 1996, 23 years after Agnes.
Three local sites are on the National Register of Historic Places: the Crum Road Bridge, the Harris Farm, and the Woodsboro and Frederick Turnpike Company Tollhouse.

insights.text: The real reason to come is the train. Time a visit to a weekend in May, June, September or October (or a Saturday in summer) and book ahead, since runs are limited.

The railroad keeps a small museum in the former Glade Valley Milling Company building across the street from the 1890s depot at 34 W. Pennsylvania Ave; pair it with the ride rather than driving out just for it.
This is a residential town rather than a downtown destination, so come for the train and the countryside scenery, not a main-street stroll.

woodsboro.one_liner: A quiet north-county town of about 1,100, birthplace of the 130-year-old Rosebud Salve brand.

fun_facts.text: Rosebud Perfume Company was founded in Woodsboro in 1895 by Dr. George F. Smith; its Smith's Rosebud Salve now sells in countries including Canada, Norway, France, Italy, China, Japan and Australia.
The town was named after Joseph Wood, to whom the land was granted in 1693, and was incorporated in 1836.

The LeGore Bridge north of town, begun in 1898 and opened in 1900, is the oldest arch bridge of any material in Frederick County and the only listed stone arch bridge still open to public road traffic there.
Merchant and philanthropist Charles Broadway Rouss, who built a Broadway dry-goods empire in New York, was born in Woodsboro in 1836.
Woodsboro's chief executive carries the old title of burgess rather than mayor.

insights.text: The real reason to come is the LeGore Bridge over the Monocacy just north of town. It is the county's oldest arch bridge and still carries everyday road traffic, best seen with the river low.

Rosebud is the find here, not a storefront experience: the 130-year-old salve brand is stocked at Ulta and Anthropologie, but the products are prepared for distribution out of town, so there is no factory tour to take.
Treat Woodsboro as a calm pass-through on the Route 194 corridor rather than a day trip; it is a residential town, so pair it with the bridge and the surrounding Frederick County countryside.
